Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test expects an IOException to be thrown when reading a truncated tar entry, but TarArchiveInputStream currently treats the unexpected EOF as a normal end-of-stream and silently stops.

Step-by-step:
- The test iterates entries via getNextTarEntry() and copies each entry’s data with IOUtils.copy(is, out). On a purposely truncated tar (COMPRESS-279.tar), the underlying stream reaches EOF before the declared entry size is fully read.
- TarArchiveInputStream.read(byte[], int, int) calculates numToRead based on the entry’s remaining size (available()). It then delegates to is.read(...). If the underlying stream has already been truncated, is.read returns -1. The current code handles this by setting hasHitEOF = true and returning -1 without throwing (lines 585–591). There is no check that entryOffset == entrySize, i.e., no detection of a truncated entry.
- IOUtils.copy interprets -1 as end-of-stream and stops copying quietly. No exception is raised, so the test continues.
- Next, getNextTarEntry() tries to advance past the current entry by calling skip(Long.MAX_VALUE), but skip simply delegates to IOUtils.skip and does not verify it actually consumed the remaining bytes of the entry (lines 193–203). With a truncated underlying stream, skip will not reach the expected end, yet no exception is thrown.
- getNextTarEntry() then attempts to read the next header record via getRecord() → readRecord(). readRecord returns null if it cannot read a full record (lines 384–392). isEOFRecord treats a null record as EOF (lines 374–376), and getRecord marks hasHitEOF and returns null (lines 356–364). Consequently, getNextTarEntry() returns null (lines 240–244) instead of signaling corruption.
- Combined, this means:
  - Unexpected EOF during entry payload read causes read(...) to return -1 rather than throwing, so copying ends silently.
  - A short read of a header block is interpreted as EOF rather than corruption.

Why the test fails:
- The test expects an IOException on truncated entries, but the code path above never throws. It silently treats the truncated data as normal end-of-stream and end-of-archive.

Likely fix points:
- In read(byte[], int, int): if totalRead == -1 while entryOffset < entrySize, throw an IOException indicating a truncated entry.
- Optionally harden getNextTarEntry()/skip: if skipping to the end of the current entry fails to consume the remaining entry bytes, throw an IOException.
- Optionally in readRecord()/getRecord()/isEOFRecord: do not treat a short read (null from readRecord) as a valid EOF record; instead throw an IOException for truncated archive blocks.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).

TarArchiveInputStream.read(byte[], int, int)
TarArchiveInputStream.readRecord()
TarArchiveInputStream.getRecord()
TarArchiveInputStream.isEOFRecord(byte[])
TarArchiveInputStream.skip(long)
